## Overview

Stacked on #63350 ("[Core] Priority scheduling: preempt for a waiting request under KV pressure"; review that first, this PR's diff is the second commit). Under priority scheduling, a high-priority request's first tokens share every step with the prefill chunks of lower-priority requests; this adds `--priority-prefill-budget-cap`, off by default, to keep those chunks out of the steps of its first tokens.

## Claims

- With the cap, prefills of a strictly lower priority, running or waiting, sit out the steps from the one in which the waiting request of the highest priority fits, or in which its KV load from a KV connector is done, while it prefills, until it has its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens (16 by default), with async scheduling as without. Decodes are never cut.
- A KV load in flight holds them out for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps only, so a load that never completes holds nothing after those.
- A waiting request that does not fit (no free running slot, or no KV cache room) holds nothing back, nor does a KV load while no running slot is free, so the prefills that will free them go on.
- Off (the default), scheduling is unchanged: the same byte-identical schedules and scheduler test results as #63350.
- Counters, `vllm:priority_prefill_held_steps` and `vllm:priority_prefill_held_tokens`, count the steps in which the cap holds lower-priority prefill back and the prefill tokens it holds back in them, at most each step's budget; they are registered only with the cap on.
- On an RTX 5060 Ti (both PRs ported to vLLM v0.32.0): behind three lower-priority prefills, a priority 0 chat turn's 16th token after 575 ms instead of 1,500 ms on v0.32.0 and 1,350 ms with #63350 alone (medians); beside 12 closed-loop agent sessions, the calls' TTFT p95 at 388 and 358 ms instead of 6,830 and 7,158 ms on v0.32.0 and 4,111 and 1,073 ms with #63350 alone.

| Scheduler | Priority 0 TTFT | Its 16th token |
|---|---|---|
| v0.32.0 | 529 ms (313–558) | 1,500 ms (1,220–1,529) |
| v0.32.0 with #63350 | 416 ms (304–556) | 1,350 ms (1,211–1,528) |
| v0.32.0 with #63350 and this change | 304 ms (292–318) | 575 ms (536–615) |

**Load.** 12 closed-loop agent sessions at priority 2 beside two calls at priority 0 for 240 s, in the same session; the calls' TTFT p50 / p95 over two runs of each (96 to 146 call turns):

| Agents' prompts | v0.32.0 | v0.32.0 with #63350 | v0.32.0 with #63350 and this change |
|---|---|---|---|
| fresh each turn | 2,244 / 6,830 ms | 716 / 4,111 ms | 236 / 388 ms |
| growing, reusing the CPU tier | 1,324 / 7,158 ms | 615 / 1,073 ms | 258 / 358 ms |

**End to end.** As in #63350, in the same five rounds: two voice calls beside 24 closed-loop coding-agent sessions replayed from Claude Code traces, every configuration in each round, medians of the five runs (1,784 ms voice-to-voice at p95 for the calls alone):

| Engine | Calls' TTFT p95 | Voice-to-voice p95 | Agents' tokens/s | Agents' TTFT p99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v0.32.0, priority scheduling | 7,786 ms | 10,523 ms | 3,304 | 107 s |
| v0.32.0 with #63350 | 1,737 ms | 5,085 ms | 3,414 | 112 s |
| v0.32.0 with #63350 and this change, 16 tokens | 364 ms | 3,094 ms | 3,298 | 105 s |
| v0.32.0 with #63350 and this change, 48 tokens | 376 ms | 2,232 ms | 3,236 | 115 s |

The window has to cover the reply's first sentence. This voice agent's replies run 23 tokens at the median and 46 at most, so at the 16-token default the first sentence's later tokens decode beside the agents' prefill again (3,094 ms), and at 48 tokens the calls' p95 is 2,232 ms, 198 ms over the calls alone plus 250 ms, with the agents at 98% of their throughput on v0.32.0.

These runs predate this revision, as the probes above do: at 16 tokens the hold lasted a 17th step in each reply that reached 16 tokens (81% of that configuration's); at 48 none reached the window (the longest had 39 tokens), so this revision changes none of those runs' steps.

**On an A100 SXM4 80 GB** (the setup of #63350's A100 runs, with #63350 and this change at a 48-token window): behind three lower-priority prefills, the priority 0 turn's tokens come 7 ms apart from its first to its 16th, against 32 ms on v0.32.0; beside 12 closed-loop agent sessions the calls' TTFT p95 is 173 ms against 3,114 ms (two runs each); end to end, the voice-to-voice p95 is 1,634 ms against 4,986 ms, as #63350 gives. At a datacenter batch, 256 requests in flight of 48 prompt and 64 output tokens in closed loop, 10% at priority 0, both changes take the priority 0 requests' TTFT p99 from 574 to 177 ms and their TPOT p50 from 28.6 to 6.9 ms, the engine's output tokens/s to 1.153 of v0.32.0's, and the priority 2 requests' TTFT p99 from 1,086 to 7,971 ms (their p50 from 341 to 283 ms): a steady stream of priority 0 requests holds lower-priority prefill back while it lasts, as the limitations below say. At vLLM's default chunking (`--max-num-batched-tokens 2048`, no long-prefill threshold), the card's best stock setting in the probes, two rounds gave v0.32.0 a voice-to-voice p95 of 4,036 and 3,289 ms and #63350 with this change 1,810 and 1,843 ms, with the agents at 100% and 101% of v0.32.0's tokens/s; what the larger chunks add is the LLM's first token behind the steps in flight when a turn arrives (412 and 414 ms at p95, against 183 and 216 ms with 512-token steps), which no scheduling rule takes back.

<details>
<summary>Each run, the load check's workload and why the KV loads matter</summary>

Voice-to-voice p95 / the calls' TTFT p95 (ms), by round (each its own draw of where the agents' sessions enter the traces):

| Engine | Round 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v0.32.0 | 9,946 / 7,040 | 10,133 / 7,941 | 10,810 / 7,786 | 12,115 / 8,965 | 10,523 / 7,786 |
| with #63350 | 6,261 / 2,407 | 5,376 / 2,120 | 4,693 / 1,602 | 4,970 / 1,737 | 5,085 / 1,539 |
| with both, 16 tokens | 3,022 / 377 | 3,100 / 350 | 2,868 / 343 | 3,192 / 364 | 3,094 / 383 |
| with both, 48 tokens | 2,174 / 344 | 2,301 / 341 | 2,189 / 403 | 2,232 / 376 | 2,397 / 443 |

An agent turn of the load check has 48 output tokens and 0 to 3 s of thought, and a prompt of 6k to 30k tokens, fresh each turn or growing by a tool result of 1k to 4k tokens so that it reuses the CPU tier; a call turns every 4 to 8 s, growing by about 30 tokens, with 16 output tokens. Between a call's turns, the agents' prefills cycle the GPU's free blocks, so the turn's prefix is evicted and loads back from the CPU tier, asynchronously. With an earlier version of the cap that did not count in-flight prefills, the calls' p95 stayed above 3 s, and every slow turn was in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` with KV to spare, as the scheduler's state logged each step showed: once its load was done, the request waited for the waiting loop, which runs only on budget the running loop leaves, and the agents' prefill chunks left none, for up to 4 s. Hence the cap counts the loads, and from the step a load is done, the request whose KV it loaded.

A load that never completes would then hold lower-priority prefill back for good, so a load in flight holds it for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps only. Holding nothing until the load is done instead cost the calls 125–131 ms at p50 and 175–202 ms at p95 in the load check (fresh and growing prompts), against holding through the load: the load's completion is seen at a step boundary, and agent prefill makes those steps several times longer.

In the prefill case, the three requests' chunks fill each step's budget while the turn decodes: from its first token to its 16th it takes 60–66 ms a token on v0.32.0, 60–65 ms with #63350 alone, which finds KV to spare here and changes nothing, and 16–20 ms with this change.
</details>

## Details

- **Which requests hold prefill back.** The running requests with fewer than `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens, those of the step in flight under async scheduling included, and those still prefilling among them; while a running slot is free, a request whose KV load is done (the waiting loop promotes it in the step, but only on budget the running loop leaves) and, for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps, a load in flight; and the waiting request of the highest priority that the waiting loop can schedule, if it fits: a free running slot, as the waiting loop checks it, and no block short as #63350's preemption counts it, deferred frees included. Only strictly lower priorities are held back, so at one priority nothing changes.
- **How.** A running prefill chunk of a lower priority gets no tokens, and vLLM skips it as any request with no new tokens; a waiting request of a lower priority is not admitted. A lower-priority request that holds KV blocks is skipped rather than waited on: the waiting loop drains those requests first, and the request whose first tokens are due may be behind it. No room is made for a waiting request the cap holds back, since it would not be admitted in the step.
- **No stall on a full running queue.** Without a free running slot, neither the waiting request nor a KV load counts, since none could be admitted or promoted; otherwise the lower-priority prefills holding the slots would sit out every step. A test with two slots, both taken while a higher-priority request loads, covers it.
- **Costs and limitations.** Lower-priority prefill makes no progress while a higher-priority request prefills or has its first tokens, so a steady stream of higher-priority requests whose first tokens overlap holds it back for as long as the stream lasts; their decodes are never cut. A load holds it for at most `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps before it is done. Per step with the cap on: one pass over the running requests and the loads in flight, and, while a request of a lower priority than the waiting request of the highest priority runs or waits (a pass over half of each waiting queue's heap tells), that request's prefix cache lookup and #63350's block count for it; the CPU cost table above gives the time. Untested: a request whose KV has loaded but finds no blocks to be promoted into (only a lower-priority request that holds KV blocks without being in flight, such as a streaming session's next chunk, can take them), while every running request is a lower-priority prefill and #63350's preemption is off.
- **Sizing the window.** `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` should cover the first output the application acts on; for a voice agent, the first sentence it hands its TTS. For this agent, 16 tokens covered 180 of 320 measured first sentences (56%) and 48 covered all 320 (median 15 tokens, p95 29, longest 39), which is why the end-to-end p95 above falls from 3,094 ms at 16 tokens to 2,232 ms at 48. A larger window holds lower-priority prefill back for more steps, so 16 suits shorter first chunks. Open question: should the default be 48, voice-sized, or stay at 16?

<details>
<summary>Changes since the last revision (9013ed433)</summary>

- **#63350's count of the blocks a preemption releases, in one pass**, cherry-picked from its branch (its notes say how), and #63350's head merged in after it, which changes no line, so that this branch holds #63350's head again: the step that preempts walks the victims' KV once. The schedules and the tests' results are unchanged; the cost table gains the F rows, that step, and with both switches, 9013ed433 → this revision: at 16 running 608 → 409 µs (main 135); at 64 running 888 → 700 µs (main 289); at 256 running 1,956 → 1,735 µs (main 1,096); with 16,000-token prompts 2,085 → 702 µs (main 77). #63350's mutations go from 34 to 35.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Changes in 9013ed433, against d1399e208</summary>

- **The first tokens count those in flight.** Under async scheduling a step is scheduled before the output of the step before it is processed, so the output tokens counted lagged one step behind those scheduled, and the hold lasted a step past `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens`. The hold now counts the request's output placeholders too, as the scheduler does for the tokens it sends the model runner: it ends in the step that schedules the first token past the window, with async scheduling as without. A synchronous step has no placeholders, so synchronous schedules are unchanged. With speculative decoding the placeholders of the step in flight include its draft tokens, so the hold can end up to that step's draft tokens before `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` are accepted.
- `test_the_first_tokens_hold_as_many_steps_under_async_scheduling` holds a 4-token window in both modes. It fails on d1399e208 under async scheduling, where the prefill is still held in the step of the fifth token, and passes now. The cap's tests go from 28 to 30; the new mutant, which leaves the placeholders out, makes it fail alone.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Changes in d1399e208, against 35f163d0d</summary>

- **Rebased on #63350's revision**, whose cuts of the per-step work it shares. With the cap on, the waiting request's prefix cache lookup is also skipped when nothing of a lower priority runs or waits, since it could then hold nothing back and no room could be made for it; `RequestQueue.has_lower_priority_than` answers for a waiting queue, a priority queue from its heap's leaves, where its largest values are. Per-step schedules are unchanged: the rebased change against the last revision, and each new commit against its parent, in 5,824 traced configurations (all seven switch sets).
- **Counters, which answer the last revision's open question on scheduler stats.** `SchedulerStats.num_prefill_held_steps` and `num_prefill_held_tokens` count, per step, the steps in which the cap holds lower-priority prefill back and the prefill tokens it holds back in them: those the running loop would have scheduled for the held chunks, within what the step has left after the chunks already held in it, so at most its budget; a held admission counts its step. The Prometheus logger exports them as `vllm:priority_prefill_held_steps` and `vllm:priority_prefill_held_tokens` when the cap is on, beside #63350's `vllm:num_priority_preemptions`.
- **The docs paragraph and the commit message** say that while higher-priority requests' first tokens are due back to back, lower-priority prefill makes no progress; the docs name the counters.
- The cap's tests go from 18 to 28; with #63350's, from 53 to 79.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Changes in 35f163d0d, against the first revision (227466714)</summary>

- A KV load in flight holds lower-priority prefill back for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps, not for the whole load: a load that never completed stopped all lower-priority prefill and admission. From the step the load is done, it holds as before.
- A lower-priority request that holds KV blocks sits out the steps of a request's first tokens too, skipped rather than waited on; the first revision let it through, against its own description.
- No room is made for a waiting request the cap holds back; the waiting request whose fit holds prefill back is the one #63350 now makes room for.
- The tests go from 27 to 53; rebased with #63350 on main `be2de7119`; the GPU numbers above are the revised changes', in one session with v0.32.0 and #63350 alone.
</details>

**Load.** 12 closed-loop agent sessions at priority 2 beside two calls at priority 0 for 240 s, in the same session; the calls' TTFT p50 / p95 over two runs of each (96 to 146 call turns):

| Agents' prompts | v0.32.0 | v0.32.0 with #63350 | v0.32.0 with #63350 and this change |

| fresh each turn | 2,244 / 6,830 ms | 716 / 4,111 ms | 236 / 388 ms |
| growing, reusing the CPU tier | 1,324 / 7,158 ms | 615 / 1,073 ms | 258 / 358 ms |

**End to end.** As in #63350, in the same five rounds: two voice calls beside 24 closed-loop coding-agent sessions replayed from Claude Code traces, every configuration in each round, medians of the five runs (1,784 ms voice-to-voice at p95 for the calls alone):

| v0.32.0, priority scheduling | 7,786 ms | 10,523 ms | 3,304 | 107 s |

The window has to cover the reply's first sentence. This voice agent's replies run 23 tokens at the median and 46 at most, so at the 16-token default the first sentence's later tokens decode beside the agents' prefill again (3,094 ms), and at 48 tokens the calls' p95 is 2,232 ms, 198 ms over the calls alone plus 250 ms, with the agents at 98% of their throughput on v0.32.0.

These runs predate this revision, as the probes above do: at 16 tokens the hold lasted a 17th step in each reply that reached 16 tokens (81% of that configuration's); at 48 none reached the window (the longest had 39 tokens), so this revision changes none of those runs' steps.

**On an A100 SXM4 80 GB** (the setup of #63350's A100 runs, with #63350 and this change at a 48-token window): behind three lower-priority prefills, the priority 0 turn's tokens come 7 ms apart from its first to its 16th, against 32 ms on v0.32.0; beside 12 closed-loop agent sessions the calls' TTFT p95 is 173 ms against 3,114 ms (two runs each); end to end, the voice-to-voice p95 is 1,634 ms against 4,986 ms, as #63350 gives. At a datacenter batch, 256 requests in flight of 48 prompt and 64 output tokens in closed loop, 10% at priority 0, both changes take the priority 0 requests' TTFT p99 from 574 to 177 ms and their TPOT p50 from 28.6 to 6.9 ms, the engine's output tokens/s to 1.153 of v0.32.0's, and the priority 2 requests' TTFT p99 from 1,086 to 7,971 ms (their p50 from 341 to 283 ms): a steady stream of priority 0 requests holds lower-priority prefill back while it lasts, as the limitations below say. At vLLM's default chunking (`--max-num-batched-tokens 2048`, no long-prefill threshold), the card's best stock setting in the probes, two rounds gave v0.32.0 a voice-to-voice p95 of 4,036 and 3,289 ms and #63350 with this change 1,810 and 1,843 ms, with the agents at 100% and 101% of v0.32.0's tokens/s; what the larger chunks add is the LLM's first token behind the steps in flight when a turn arrives (412 and 414 ms at p95, against 183 and 216 ms with 512-token steps), which no scheduling rule takes back.

<details>
<summary>Each run, the load check's workload and why the KV loads matter</summary>

Voice-to-voice p95 / the calls' TTFT p95 (ms), by round (each its own draw of where the agents' sessions enter the traces):

| Engine | Round 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v0.32.0 | 9,946 / 7,040 | 10,133 / 7,941 | 10,810 / 7,786 | 12,115 / 8,965 | 10,523 / 7,786 |
| with #63350 | 6,261 / 2,407 | 5,376 / 2,120 | 4,693 / 1,602 | 4,970 / 1,737 | 5,085 / 1,539 |
| with both, 16 tokens | 3,022 / 377 | 3,100 / 350 | 2,868 / 343 | 3,192 / 364 | 3,094 / 383 |
| with both, 48 tokens | 2,174 / 344 | 2,301 / 341 | 2,189 / 403 | 2,232 / 376 | 2,397 / 443 |

An agent turn of the load check has 48 output tokens and 0 to 3 s of thought, and a prompt of 6k to 30k tokens, fresh each turn or growing by a tool result of 1k to 4k tokens so that it reuses the CPU tier; a call turns every 4 to 8 s, growing by about 30 tokens, with 16 output tokens. Between a call's turns, the agents' prefills cycle the GPU's free blocks, so the turn's prefix is evicted and loads back from the CPU tier, asynchronously. With an earlier version of the cap that did not count in-flight prefills, the calls' p95 stayed above 3 s, and every slow turn was in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` with KV to spare, as the scheduler's state logged each step showed: once its load was done, the request waited for the waiting loop, which runs only on budget the running loop leaves, and the agents' prefill chunks left none, for up to 4 s. Hence the cap counts the loads, and from the step a load is done, the request whose KV it loaded.

A load that never completes would then hold lower-priority prefill back for good, so a load in flight holds it for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps only. Holding nothing until the load is done instead cost the calls 125–131 ms at p50 and 175–202 ms at p95 in the load check (fresh and growing prompts), against holding through the load: the load's completion is seen at a step boundary, and agent prefill makes those steps several times longer.

In the prefill case, the three requests' chunks fill each step's budget while the turn decodes: from its first token to its 16th it takes 60–66 ms a token on v0.32.0, 60–65 ms with #63350 alone, which finds KV to spare here and changes nothing, and 16–20 ms with this change.
</details>

## Details

- **Which requests hold prefill back.** The running requests with fewer than `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens, those of the step in flight under async scheduling included, and those still prefilling among them; while a running slot is free, a request whose KV load is done (the waiting loop promotes it in the step, but only on budget the running loop leaves) and, for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps, a load in flight; and the waiting request of the highest priority that the waiting loop can schedule, if it fits: a free running slot, as the waiting loop checks it, and no block short as #63350's preemption counts it, deferred frees included. Only strictly lower priorities are held back, so at one priority nothing changes.
- **How.** A running prefill chunk of a lower priority gets no tokens, and vLLM skips it as any request with no new tokens; a waiting request of a lower priority is not admitted. A lower-priority request that holds KV blocks is skipped rather than waited on: the waiting loop drains those requests first, and the request whose first tokens are due may be behind it. No room is made for a waiting request the cap holds back, since it would not be admitted in the step.
- **No stall on a full running queue.** Without a free running slot, neither the waiting request nor a KV load counts, since none could be admitted or promoted; otherwise the lower-priority prefills holding the slots would sit out every step. A test with two slots, both taken while a higher-priority request loads, covers it.
- **Costs and limitations.** Lower-priority prefill makes no progress while a higher-priority request prefills or has its first tokens, so a steady stream of higher-priority requests whose first tokens overlap holds it back for as long as the stream lasts; their decodes are never cut. A load holds it for at most `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps before it is done. Per step with the cap on: one pass over the running requests and the loads in flight, and, while a request of a lower priority than the waiting request of the highest priority runs or waits (a pass over half of each waiting queue's heap tells), that request's prefix cache lookup and #63350's block count for it; the CPU cost table above gives the time. Untested: a request whose KV has loaded but finds no blocks to be promoted into (only a lower-priority request that holds KV blocks without being in flight, such as a streaming session's next chunk, can take them), while every running request is a lower-priority prefill and #63350's preemption is off.
- **Sizing the window.** `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` should cover the first output the application acts on; for a voice agent, the first sentence it hands its TTS. For this agent, 16 tokens covered 180 of 320 measured first sentences (56%) and 48 covered all 320 (median 15 tokens, p95 29, longest 39), which is why the end-to-end p95 above falls from 3,094 ms at 16 tokens to 2,232 ms at 48. A larger window holds lower-priority prefill back for more steps, so 16 suits shorter first chunks. Open question: should the default be 48, voice-sized, or stay at 16?

@@ -46,6 +46,17 @@ You can monitor the number of preemption requests through Prometheus metrics exp
 
 In vLLM V1, the default preemption mode is `RECOMPUTE` rather than `SWAP`, as recomputation has lower overhead in the V1 architecture.
 
+### Preemption for Higher-Priority Requests
+
+With `--scheduling-policy priority`, a waiting request does not preempt running requests by default: a high-priority request that finds the KV cache full waits until running requests of a lower priority finish, or until one of them is preempted because a running request cannot grow. `--max-priority-preemptions-per-step N` (0, off, by default) lets the waiting request of the highest priority that can be scheduled preempt up to `N` running requests of a strictly lower priority in a step when the KV cache lacks room for its whole sequence: in the order the scheduler preempts in, the lowest priority first and the latest arrival within it, and none if `N` would not make room. The room is net of the request's prefix cache hits, and it counts the blocks the running requests take until the preempted requests' blocks are freed. They resume like any preempted request once in-flight prefills of a higher priority have the blocks they still need, and the Prometheus counter `vllm:num_priority_preemptions` counts them.
+
+`--priority-prefill-budget-cap` (off by default) keeps prefills of a strictly lower priority, running or waiting, out of the steps of a request's first tokens: from the step in which the waiting request of the highest priority fits (a free running slot and KV cache room for its whole sequence), or in which its KV load from a KV connector is done, while it prefills, until it has its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` output tokens (16 by default). A KV load in flight holds them out for its first `--priority-prefill-budget-cap-tokens` steps only, so a load that never completes holds nothing after those. Decodes are never cut, a request that does not fit holds nothing back, and nothing is held back while no running slot is free. While higher-priority requests' first tokens are due back to back, lower-priority prefill makes no progress. The Prometheus counters `vllm:priority_prefill_held_steps` and `vllm:priority_prefill_held_tokens` count the steps the cap holds and the prefill tokens it holds back in them.
+
+```bash
+vllm serve <model> --scheduling-policy priority \
+    --max-priority-preemptions-per-step 2 --priority-prefill-budget-cap
+```
+
 ## Chunked Prefill
 
 Chunked prefill allows vLLM to process large prefills in smaller chunks and batch them together with decode requests. This feature helps improve both throughput and latency by better balancing compute-bound (prefill) and memory-bound (decode) operations.

+        self._load_hold_start = {

+            for req in self._inflight_prefills

+        request: Request | None,
+        hit: tuple[tuple[list[KVCacheBlock], ...], int] | None,
+        hold_priority: int | None,
+    ) -> int | None:
+        """With the budget cap, the highest priority whose first tokens hold
+        lower-priority prefill back in this step: `hold_priority`, and that of
+        the waiting `request` (whose prefix-cache hit is `hit`) once it fits,
+        deferred frees counted, while a running slot is free."""
+        if not self.priority_prefill_budget_cap:
+            return None
+        priorities = [] if hold_priority is None else [hold_priority]

+            request is not None
+            and self._running_slot_free()
+            and self._num_blocks_short(request, hit)
+            <= self._num_released_blocks([], hit)

+        back, once, and the prefill tokens it holds back in it: those the running

+        `budget` the step has left less the chunks held before it, which took
+        nothing from it. So a step's held tokens are at most its budget."""

+            self._prefill_held_step = self.current_step

+        self._prefill_held_step_tokens += num_tokens

+    def _running_slot_free(self) -> bool:
+        """Whether a running slot is free: a waiting request, or one whose KV
+        load is done, needs one to be promoted, and with none free, holding
+        prefill back would only stall the running requests."""

+    def _local_prefix_hit(

+        without its KV events; None if it looks up none."""

+            request.num_computed_tokens

+            return None

+    def _make_room(

+        hit: tuple[tuple[list[KVCacheBlock], ...], int] | None,
+        timestamp: float,
+    ) -> set[Request]:
+        """Preempt running requests of a lower priority than the waiting
+        `request` until it is no block short, and return them. They go in the
+        order the running loop preempts in, the highest priority value first and
+        the latest arrival among equals, which spares older work: as few as make
+        it fit, at most `max_priority_preemptions_per_step`, and none if that
+        many would not. The room counts the blocks the running decodes take until

+            return set()

+    def _num_blocks_short(
+        self,
+        request: Request,
+        hit: tuple[tuple[list[KVCacheBlock], ...], int] | None,

+        """Free blocks the waiting `request` lacks to be admitted with its whole

+
+    def _make_room_remaining_blocks(
+        self,
+        request: Request,
+        hit: tuple[tuple[list[KVCacheBlock], ...], int] | None,
+    ) -> int:
+        """Blocks the waiting `request` still needs for its whole remaining
+        sequence, as allocate_slots admits it: net of its prefix-cache hit `hit`,
+        whose blocks other requests hold take none and whose blocks in the free

+            self.kv_cache_manager.empty_kv_cache_blocks.blocks,

+    def _num_growth_blocks(self, request: Request, num_steps: int) -> int:

+        next `num_steps` steps: a decode's tokens (and lookahead) may start

+        return self.kv_cache_manager.coordinator.get_num_blocks_to_allocate(
+            request_id=request.request_id,
+            num_tokens=min(
+                num_tokens_main_model + self.num_lookahead_tokens, self.max_model_len
+            ),
+            new_computed_blocks=self.kv_cache_manager.empty_kv_cache_blocks.blocks,
+            num_encoder_tokens=0,
+            total_computed_tokens=request.num_computed_tokens,
+            num_local_computed_tokens=request.num_computed_tokens,
+            num_tokens_main_model=num_tokens_main_model,
+        )

+    def _num_released_blocks(
+        self,
+        victims: list[Request],
+        hit: tuple[tuple[list[KVCacheBlock], ...], int] | None,
+    ) -> int:
+        """Blocks back in the free pool by the next step once `victims` are
+        preempted: those whose every holder is a victim or a deferred free, which

+        blocks: dict[int, KVCacheBlock] = {}

+            groups.extend(self.kv_cache_manager.get_blocks(victim.request_id).blocks)
+        block_pool = self.kv_cache_manager.block_pool

+        # released where it is seen, and only a shared block's holders are

+        num_blocks = 0
